name_variants: Hye-ch'o; Huichao; Hye Ch'o; 慧超; 惠超
profession_role: Buddhist monk; pilgrim; translator
religious_affiliation: Buddhism (Esoteric/Vajrayana; disciple of Vajrabodhi and Amoghavajra)
institution_org: Juefu Temple (Chang'an); Dryuan Puti Temple (Mt Wutai)
india_connection: Pilgrimage to the Five Indias c. 723-727 (sea out via Guangzhou, land back via Central Asia/Persia); visited Kushinagara, Varanasi, Rajagrha, Bodhgaya, Lumbini, Kashmir, Gandhara
korea_connection: Silla-born; never returned to Korea; active in Tang; among Amoghavajra's six great disciples; later in Japanese Shingon lineage
travel_summary: Departed Guangzhou by sea (c. 719 or 723); toured the Five Indias; reached Nishapur (Persia); returned overland via Pamir/Central Asia; account ends at Kucha, Nov 727
evidence_of_influence: Wang ocheonchukguk jeon (往五天竺國傳), the sole surviving 8th-c. East Asian record of India/Central Asia; Dunhuang ms. (Pelliot 1908), Bibliothèque nationale de France
historical_significance: First Korean recorded to have travelled to India by sea and returned overland leaving a written record; 'world's oldest of the four great travelogues' per Korean scholarship
notes: Travel dates conflict across sources (719-727 vs 723-727/728; '730경' per our-history-net). Standard Korean dates 704-787 (Korean Wikipedia, NIKH-adjacent sources, 인천in); birth c. 700 / death 780 appear in older scholarship - kept as variant. Author identification with Amoghavajra's Silla disciple is scholarly consensus (Takakusu).

name_variants: Wŏnch'ŭk; Wonchuk; Wuan-tshe (Tibetan); Ximing dashi; 圓測
profession_role: Buddhist monk; Yogacara scholar; abbot
india_connection: Studied Indian Yogacara doctrine (Vasubandhu's texts) via Xuanzang's translations in Chang'an; never travelled to India
korea_connection: Silla royal family (grandson of King Chinp'yong per some accounts); ordained at 15 in Silla before going to Tang
travel_summary: NULL (Silla->Tang c. 627 only; lived in Chang'an)
evidence_of_influence: Commentaries (e.g., on Samdhinirmocana-sutra) studied and quoted in Tibetan doxographies; long-standing rivalry with Kuiji
historical_significance: One of the most influential Silla monks in Tang China; his works transmitted to Tibet
notes: Dates 613-696 per John Powers (JIABS); some accounts differ slightly.

name_variants: Wonhyo; Wŏn-hyo; 元曉; Haedong bosal; 'Jinna bosal' epithet in China
profession_role: Buddhist philosopher-monk; author; popularizer; founder of Haedongjong
india_connection: Deeply studied Indian-origin texts, esp. the Awakening of Faith (attributed to Asvaghosa); wrote famous Haedong-so commentaries; legend of an aborted trip to Tang/India
korea_connection: Silla native; tutored many Silla monks; works transmitted to Tang and Japan
travel_summary: Legend (hagiography): while travelling to Tang with Ŭisang, awakened overnight in a cave ('mind only') and never went abroad; no India journey recorded
evidence_of_influence: Haedong-so commentaries studied in Tang/Japan; called 'Jinna bosal' in China (equated with Indian logician Dignaga); T'ong pulgyo synthesis
historical_significance: Korea's greatest Buddhist philosopher; synthesized Indian/Chinese Buddhist thought for Korea
notes: Person and works verified; the cave legend is traditional hagiography. Relationship to India is intellectual, not physical.

nationality_region: KOREAN (Silla; born Ungcheon, former Baekje territory)
profession_role: Buddhist monk; commentator; one of Silla's 'Three/Four Great Writers'
institution_org: Samrangsa (三郎寺); made Kukro (national elder) by King Sinmun
india_connection: Authored commentaries on Indian-derived sutras (Three Pure Land sutras incl. the Smaller Sukhavativyuha; Golden Light Sutra) without travelling to India
korea_connection: Silla monk under King Sinmun (r. 681-692); works survive via Japanese holdings
travel_summary: NULL
evidence_of_influence: Sam Mireukgyeong so (三彌勒經疏) and Muryangsugyong yonuisulmunchan survive; the latter long studied in Japan; ~40 works recorded, 3 extant
historical_significance: Major Silla exegete of Indian Buddhist scriptural heritage; bridge from Baekje-refugee traditions into Unified Silla scholarship
notes: Exact dates unrecorded; ordained at 18; lived during King Sinmun's reign.

name_variants: Taehyon; Tae-hyŏn; 太賢; 大賢
profession_role: Buddhist monk; Yogacara commentator; one of Silla's Four Great Writers
religious_affiliation: Buddhism (Yogacara; later revered as founder of Goryeo Yugajong)
india_connection: Commented on Xuanzang/Dharmapala-derived Cheng Weishi Lun (Indian Yogacara thought); no India travel
korea_connection: Silla monk; 52 works recorded, 5 extant
travel_summary: NULL
evidence_of_influence: Seong yusik non hakki (成唯識論學記) and Daeseung gisillon naeui yaktamgi (Awakening of Faith commentary); Beommanggyeong gojeokki (Brahma's Net Sutra)
historical_significance: Key Silla interpreter of Indian-origin Yogacara texts; foundational figure claimed by early Goryeo Yugajong
notes: Dates approximate; placed in King Gyeongdeok's reign (742-765) by tradition; some scholars date him later.

name_variants: Mallananda; 摩羅難陀; 摩羅難陁
nationality_region: UNCERTAIN (Western Regions/Serindia; some scholars argue Indian; came via Eastern Jin China)
profession_role: Buddhist monk ('foreign monk' 胡僧)
india_connection: If Indian (per some scholars, e.g., Lee Sang-ho 1960), the first Indian Buddhist to reach Korea; at minimum connected to Indian Buddhism via Central Asian monastic networks of the Jin period
korea_connection: Arrived Baekje 384 (9th month, King Chimnyu's 1st year); received by the king; Buddhism 'began from this' (Samguk Sagi); temple built 385
travel_summary: Came from Eastern Jin territory to Baekje by sea, 384 CE; no detailed itinerary preserved
evidence_of_influence: Samguk Sagi (sg_024r_0100_0030) and Samguk Yusa records; both mark 384 as the start of Baekje Buddhism
historical_significance: Traditional founder of Baekje Buddhism; earliest documented Buddhist arrival in Korean history
notes: Origin debated: db.history.go.kr (Samguk Sagi) notes '흔히 서역 출신으로 추정' with a minority view identifying him as an Indian monk (이상호 1960); encykorea describes him as '인도의 승려' (Gandhara-born per en-wiki); arrived via Eastern Jin. Sanskrit reconstruction of the name not attested in sources.

name_variants: Hŏ Hwang-ok; Huh Hwang-ok; 許黃玉; Queen of Suro of Geumgwan Gaya
indian_local_name_variants: (legendary) from 'Ayuta' (아유타), often equated with Ayodhya, India
nationality_region: LEGENDARY (said to be from Ayuta; disputed: Ayodhya vs other readings)
profession_role: Queen consort of King Suro of Geumgwan Gaya (legendary)
india_connection: Legend: came by ship from Ayuta (often equated with Ayodhya, India) in 48 CE bearing gifts (twin-fish symbols); married King Suro
korea_connection: Ancestress of the Gaya Heo clan; tomb at Gimhae royal tombs; centre of modern India-Korea memory culture
travel_summary: Legendary sea voyage from Ayuta in 48 CE; no contemporary record beyond Samguk Yusa/Garakguk-gi tradition (compiled centuries later)
evidence_of_influence: Samguk Yusa (Garakguk-gi) narrative; modern movements (Kim Byung-mo's Ayodhya/twin-fish thesis) vs scholarly skepticism (Mohan, Kim Tae-sik: narrative reworked in Middle Silla/Goryeo)
historical_significance: Symbol of India-Korea relations; also the most contested India-Korea connection - flagged as legend with historiographical caveats
notes: Scholarly debate: Kim Byung-mo's Ayodhya thesis vs Mohan/Kim Tae-sik skepticism (Goryeo-era narrative reworking); 'brother Jangyoo Hwasang' myth is a later addition (Ko Il-hong, SNU).

name_variants: King Suro; Kim Suro; 首露王; 金首露
nationality_region: LEGENDARY (founder of Geumgwan Gaya, now Gimhae, Korea)
profession_role: King (legendary founder)
india_connection: Legendary: married Heo Hwang-ok, said to be from 'Ayuta' (often read as Ayodhya, India); six-egg origin myth
korea_connection: Ancestor figure of the Gimhae Kim clan
travel_summary: Legend only; no physical journey recorded for Suro himself (the 'travel' is his legendary wife's); narrative survives via Garakguk-gi in Samguk Yusa
evidence_of_influence: Same corpus as Heo Hwang-ok; modern India ties derive from the marriage legend
historical_significance: Founder-king of Geumgwan Gaya; central to the Ayodhya-connection myth debates
notes: No contemporary record; Samguk Yusa (13th c.) is the earliest source via Garakguk-gi. Legendary reign 42-199 CE.

name_variants: Il-yeon; Ilyon; Ichinen (Japanese); 一然; born Kim Gyeon-myeong
profession_role: Buddhist monk; historian; author
institution_org: Inheungsa; Unmunsa; posthumous title Bogak Guksa
india_connection: Compiled the Samguk Yusa (三國遺事, c. 1283-1287), the primary medieval Korean source preserving the Marananta, Gyeomik, Heo Hwang-ok and Suro traditions about Indian contact
korea_connection: Goryeo monk; author of Korea's most important historical compendium after Kim Busik's Samguk Sagi
travel_summary: NULL
evidence_of_influence: Samguk Yusa is the source for most legendary India-Korea traditions studied today
historical_significance: Sole compiler of many early India-Korea narratives; critical for the Marananta/Heo Hwang-ok/Suro historiography
notes: Wrote ~80 volumes; only Samguk Yusa survives.

profession_role: Buddhist monk; Esoteric (Milgyo) master
institution_org: Tang (Chang'an) milieu; 'Six Disciples of Amoghavajra' orbit
india_connection: Inherited Indian-origin esoteric teaching of Amoghavajra; introduced to Silla the Buddha-Usnisa Dharani tradition
korea_connection: Carried Amoghavajra-lineage Vajrayana back to Silla (King Wonseong era, c. 789)
travel_summary: NULL (Silla->Tang->Silla; no India travel recorded)
evidence_of_influence: KCI scholarship traces Goryeo Buddha-Usnisa practice halls to the Bukong->Hyeil lineage; EncyKorea '밀교' lists Silla 惠日 among esoteric monks
historical_significance: Key conduit of Indian-origin esoteric Buddhism to late Silla
notes: DO NOT confuse with (a) Goryeo Hwaeom monk Gyeoleung (courtesy name 慧日), (b) late-Goryeo Jeju poet-monk 慧日, or (c) a Japanese monk 惠日 (623).

profession_role: Monk; Vinaya (Lu) scholar-translator
institution_org: Sangana Great Vinaya Monastery (常伽那大律寺), Central India; Heungnyunsa (Baekje)
india_connection: Travelled to India by sea in 526 (Seongwang 4); studied Sanskrit 5 years at Sangana; returned 531 with Indian monk Baedalta bearing Sanskrit Abhidharma and Five-Part Vinaya texts
korea_connection: Translated 72 volumes of Vinaya with 28 monks; founded the Baekje Vinaya school
travel_summary: Sea route out (526) -> Central India (Sangana, 5 years) -> return 531 via sea with Indian Vinaya master Baedalta
evidence_of_influence: Recorded in Korean tradition (Samguk Yusa and later compilations); encyclopedia entries on the Baekje Vinaya school
historical_significance: Baekje's greatest documented Indian pilgrim; brought Vinaya and Sanskrit scholarship to Korea
notes: Recorded in Korean Buddhist tradition; surviving sources are later compilations.

name_variants: 倍達多 (modern Sanskrit reconstruction not attested)
profession_role: Indian Tripitaka master (三藏)
india_connection: Indian monk who accompanied Gyeomik to Baekje in 531, carrying Sanskrit Abhidharma and Vinaya texts
korea_connection: His arrival in Baekje (531) supported the establishment of the Vinaya school
travel_summary: India -> Baekje by sea, 531 CE (with Gyeomik)
evidence_of_influence: Korean Buddhist tradition (via Gyeomik narrative); encyclopedia entries on Baekje Vinaya
historical_significance: Attested Indian monk physically present in Korea; rare documented 6th-century India-to-Korea movement
notes: Hanja given in tradition; do not assert a specific Sanskrit reconstruction.

profession_role: Pilgrim monk
india_connection: From Chang'an went to India, stayed at Nalanda, studied sutras and died there aged 70+
korea_connection: Recorded in Yijing's Da Tang Xiyu qiufa gaoseng zhuan (大唐西域求法高僧傳) as a Silla person (新罗人)
travel_summary: Silla -> Chang'an -> Nalanda (Central India); died at Nalanda
evidence_of_influence: Yijing's 7th-century record (contemporary witness); modern Korean scholarship (KCI)
historical_significance: Contemporary 7th-century testimony of a Silla monk resident at Nalanda
notes: Recorded by Yijing (義淨), who visited India 671-695.

profession_role: Pilgrim monk
india_connection: Travelled to India, dwelt at Bodhi temple (Bodhgaya) and Nalanda; died there aged ~60; his Sanskrit manuscripts were seen at Nalanda by Yijing's party
korea_connection: Silla monk; noted in a colophon as '新罗僧慧业写记' at the Buddha-tooth tree
travel_summary: Silla -> India (Bodhgaya, Nalanda); died in India
evidence_of_influence: Yijing's Da Tang Xiyu qiufa gaoseng zhuan
historical_significance: Physical presence of a Silla monk at Bodhgaya/Nalanda attested in Yijing's record
notes: NULL

profession_role: Pilgrim monk
india_connection: Travelled to India; returned to Tang; died in China
korea_connection: Silla monk recorded among the Silla contingent in Yijing's compilation
travel_summary: Silla -> India -> Tang (died in China)
evidence_of_influence: Yijing's Da Tang Xiyu qiufa gaoseng zhuan
historical_significance: Part of the documented 7th-century Silla cohort at Indian Buddhist sites
notes: NULL

profession_role: Pilgrim monk
india_connection: Accompanied Chinese monk Xuanzhao (玄照) in the Zhenguan era to Dajue Temple (Bodhgaya); died sick there in his 40s
korea_connection: Silla monk recorded in Yijing's compilation
travel_summary: Silla -> India (with Xuanzhao) -> died at Bodhgaya
evidence_of_influence: Yijing's Da Tang Xiyu qiufa gaoseng zhuan
historical_significance: Documented Silla monk who died at Bodhgaya in the 7th century
notes: NULL

profession_role: Pilgrim monk
india_connection: Went to India (recorded with the Silla contingent in Yijing)
korea_connection: Silla monk recorded in Yijing's compilation
travel_summary: Silla -> India
evidence_of_influence: Yijing's Da Tang Xiyu qiufa gaoseng zhuan
historical_significance: Part of the documented 7th-century Silla cohort in India
notes: NULL

nationality_region: KOREAN (Silla; reading per Kim Bok-soon; Yijing wrote 高麗)
profession_role: Pilgrim monk
india_connection: Included in Yijing's Da Tang Xiyu qiufa gaoseng zhuan among Korean monks
korea_connection: Korean monk; linked to the 高麗-雞貴 identification question
travel_summary: Korea -> (per Yijing) India route network
evidence_of_influence: Yijing's Da Tang Xiyu qiufa gaoseng zhuan; KCI scholarship (Kim Bok-soon)
historical_significance: Contributes to the documented Korean monastic presence in Yijing's India network
notes: Identification as Silla vs Koguryo/Goryeo debated (Yijing wrote '高麗'). Note: Yijing's 雞貴 gloss ('矩矩吒是雞，醫說羅是貴，即高麗國也') is an ethnonym for the Korean people, not a monk - the former P-0019 record was removed on that basis.

profession_role: Esoteric Buddhist monk
institution_org: Tang (Chang'an) milieu; studied under Hyegwa (慧果)
india_connection: Went to Tang with Hyeil (惠日, c. 789, King Wonseong era); went to Central India and died in Tibet
korea_connection: Silla esoteric monk; part of the Amoghavajra-lineage transmission to Silla
travel_summary: Silla -> Tang -> Central India -> Tibet (death)
evidence_of_influence: KCI scholarship (Ko Young-seop on Lamotte); EncyKorea '밀교'
historical_significance: Documented late-8th-century Silla monk who reached Central India
notes: NULL

profession_role: Monk
india_connection: Travelled to India via Tang (King Gyeongdeok era, 742-765); returned to Tang and died in China
korea_connection: Unified Silla monk
travel_summary: Silla -> Tang -> India -> Tang (death in China)
evidence_of_influence: KCI scholarship (Ko Young-seop on Lamotte)
historical_significance: Documented 8th-century Unified Silla monk who reached India
notes: Transcription varies (원표/元表).

profession_role: Monk
india_connection: Followed Chinese monk Sengche (僧哲) to Sri Lanka and was ordained there (South Asian connection; not mainland India)
korea_connection: Goguryeo monk
travel_summary: Goguryeo -> (via China) -> Sri Lanka; ordained there
evidence_of_influence: KCI scholarship (Ko Young-seop on Lamotte)
historical_significance: Documented Korean monk in the South Asian monastic world (Sri Lanka) in the 7th century
notes: Connection is to Sri Lanka rather than mainland India; direction of influence for India-Korea exchange uncertain.

name_variants: Jikong (指空); Shikong; Śūnyadiśya-Dhyānabhadra; Zhikong Chanxian
profession_role: Indian Buddhist master; Seon/Chan patriarch
india_connection: Born in Magadha (Indian royal family per tradition); ordained at Nalanda; famous in India before leaving
korea_connection: Invited by King Ch'ungsuk (met at Mongol court); came to Goryeo 1326; founded Hoeamsa 1328 (reportedly modeled on Nalanda); influenced Korean Seon students incl. Naong Hyegeun and Muhak Chach'o; King Kongmin later sent his relics to Goryeo
travel_summary: Magadha -> (Tibet) -> Yuan China -> Goryeo (1326) -> Yuan China; died 1363 (relics sent to Goryeo)
evidence_of_influence: Hagiographical and scholastic records; temple foundation (Hoeamsa 1328); lineage transmission to Naong and Muhak
historical_significance: The last great Indian monk active in Korea; key figure in late-Goryeo Seon formation
notes: Biography contains hagiographical elements (Indian royal family per tradition; ordained at Nalanda at age 8, completed training at 19 - per Yangju Hoeamsa museum and stele tradition). Core facts standard across sources: Magadha -> Yuan Dadu -> Goryeo 1326 (Ch'ungsuk era) -> Dadu Beopwonsa; died 1363; Hoeamsa stupa erected 1372 (壬子; stele text by Yi Saek).

profession_role: Seon monk
india_connection: Received bodhisattva precepts from the Indian master Dhyānabhadra (Jikong) at age 7 (at Sungsusa) and met him again in Yuan China at age 38, receiving Jikong's exhortation to return to Korea
korea_connection: Major Goryeo Seon master; successor-influence of Jikong's lineage
travel_summary: Travelled to Yuan China (not India); India connection entirely mediated through Jikong
evidence_of_influence: KCI scholarship (Ko Young-seop on Lamotte) documenting the Jikong-Naong relationship
historical_significance: The channel through which the Indian monk Dhyānabhadra's teaching entered mainstream Goryeo Seon
notes: No personal travel to India; relationship mediated via the Indian master Jikong.

name_variants: Yi Sugwang; Lee Soo-kwang; pen name Jibong (芝峰)
profession_role: Scholar-official; encyclopedist; envoy to Ming China
india_connection: Compiled the Foreign Countries (外國) section of Jibong yuseol with entries on India-linked polities - Bengal (榜葛剌), Ceylon (錫蘭山), Calicut (古俚) - based on Ming-era Chinese sources; among the earliest organized channels of India-related geographic knowledge into Joseon
korea_connection: National cultural figure; Jibong yuseol (1614) is the foundational Korean encyclopedia
travel_summary: Travelled to Ming China (1609-11); never to India
evidence_of_influence: Jibong yuseol Foreign Countries section; Yeungnam University Press scholarly edition
historical_significance: First systematic Joseon-era encyclopedic intake of Indian subcontinent geography
notes: India content enters via Chinese-world geography, not direct observation.

profession_role: Silhak scholar; encyclopedist
india_connection: UNCERTAIN - his encyclopedia Oju yŏnmun changjŏn san'go (60 books, 1,417 topics; ~80 items on Western learning and world geography) plausibly contains India-related entries, but no specific India entry was verified in this pilot
korea_connection: One of Joseon's greatest encyclopedists; Oju is a national cultural monument
travel_summary: Did not travel abroad
evidence_of_influence: NULL (India-specific entries not yet located)
historical_significance: Representative late-Joseon encyclopedic frame for absorbing world (incl. Asian) knowledge
notes: Born 1788-08-05, died 1856-05-16 (Korean Wikipedia; lunar dates). Follow-up needed: locate India entries (e.g., 天竺, 佛國) inside Oju itself.

profession_role: Silhak philosopher; geographer; encyclopedist
india_connection: Authored Jiguyŏn'gu (地球典要, 1857), a world-geography compendium introducing the Indian subcontinent to Korean readers, compiled chiefly from Xu Jiyu's Yinghuan zhilüe (瀛寰志略) and Wei Yuan's Haiguo tuzhi (海國圖志)
korea_connection: Major Silhak figure; pre-modern Korean systematizer of world geography
travel_summary: Never travelled outside Korea
evidence_of_influence: EncyKorea entry on Jiguyŏn'gu (E0054094) confirming work, sources and scope; KCI scholarship (Sohn Yong-Taek)
historical_significance: First complete Korean-language world geography including India's place in the Asian world
notes: India appears as part of the world-region survey, not a standalone study.

name_variants: Yi Neunghwa; courtesy name Chahyŏn; pen names Kanjŏng, Sanghyŏn, Munŭng kŏsa
profession_role: Historian; religious scholar; folklorist ('father of Korean religious studies'); school principal
institution_org: Hanseong Law-French School (principal); Chosŏn History Compilation Committee; Jungang Buddhist College lecturer
india_connection: In Chosŏn Pulgyo T'ongsa (朝鮮佛敎通史, 1918) wrote the first comprehensive Korean Buddhist history tracing Korean Buddhism to its Indian origins; his comparative-religion framework (Paekkyo hoet'ong, 1912) engaged Indian religions
korea_connection: National religious historian; pioneer of Korean religious studies
travel_summary: Visited Japan once on official inspection (1906-07); never India
evidence_of_influence: Chosŏn Pulgyo T'ongsa (Internet Archive scan); EncyKorea and AKS biographical entries
historical_significance: Definitive early-20th-century account of Korean Buddhism's Indian-rooted history
notes: Date discrepancy resolved: 1869-1943 per EncyKorea/AKS (Internet Archive's '1865-1945' is an error). Colonial-era record includes pro-Japanese designations.

name_variants: Choi Nam-sun; pen name Yuktang (六堂)
profession_role: Enlightenment thinker; historian; publisher; magazine editor
religious_affiliation: None (wrote on Buddhism as national culture)
india_connection: (a) Met Tagore at his Imperial University lecture in Tokyo, 1916 (first documented Korean-intellectual contact with Tagore); (b) in Chosŏn Pulgyo (1930, written for the Korean delegation to the Hawai'i Pan-Pacific Buddhist Youth Conference) argued Buddhism reached Korea directly from India/Xiyu via a 'northern route', independent of the China route; coined the scheme: India's introductory Buddhism, China's sectional Buddhism, Korea's conclusive Buddhism
korea_connection: National enlightenment icon; Dangun/Bulham culture theory
travel_summary: Studied in Japan (Tokyo); met Tagore there 1916; never visited India
evidence_of_influence: budreview.com profile (Kim Young-jin 2013) quoting the India/Xiyu direct-route claim; beopbo.com on Chosŏn Pulgyo (2004); EncyKorea '통불교사상'
historical_significance: Cast Korea as the culmination (not periphery) of India-originated Buddhism in world civilizational history
notes: Beware the widespread 'Yuktang requested Song of the Defeated' myth - corrected by Hong Eun-taek (the request was made by Chin Hak-mun).

profession_role: Poet; novelist; playwright; essayist; educator; first Asian Nobel laureate in Literature (1913)
india_connection: India's national poet; the central Indian figure of Korea's literary imagination in the colonial era
korea_connection: Signed a 6-line English message dated 1929-03-28 (Tokyo) later known as 'The Lamp of the East' (동방의 등불), delivered at Yokohama departure for the Korean people; published in Dong-a Ilbo Apr 1929, translated by Chu Yo-han; planned a Korea lecture in June 1929 (cancelled for health); sent 'The Song of the Defeated' to Chin Hak-mun in 1916 (published in Ch'ŏngch'un Nov 1917); met Ch'oe Nam-sŏn and Chin Hak-mun in Tokyo/Yokohama 1916
travel_summary: Visited Japan five times (1916-1929) and China once (1924); never set foot in Korea despite two planned contacts; met Korean students in person in Tokyo/Yokohama 1916
evidence_of_influence: Dong-a Ilbo archival record; Hong Eun-taek's studies (2012, 2014); Choi Seong-woo's rhetorical analysis (2022); Kim Ujo (2014) in 인도연구; 2011 bust at Daehak-ro (gift of the Indian government)
historical_significance: The single most important Indian figure in Korean cultural memory of this period; his 'lamp' message became a national symbol of hope
notes: The famous 15-line 'poem' is a patchwork: Tagore's actual message was a 6-line English note (an apology for declining the lecture request), translated into 4 Korean lines by Chu Yo-han (Apr 1929); Gitanjali #35 was appended and 'Korea' inserted in a closing line Tagore never wrote (likely from 세계명시선 1977); circulated in 2002/2003 textbooks and inscribed under the 2011 bust. First poem actually sent to Koreans: 'The Song of the Defeated' (Fruit-Gathering no. 85, Jan 1916).

profession_role: Student in Tokyo; translator
india_connection: Met Tagore twice at Yokohama during Tagore's 1916 Japan visit; requested and received 'The Song of the Defeated'
korea_connection: Translated and published the poem (under censorship-adjusted title 「쫓긴 이의 노래」) in Ch'ŏngch'un No. 11 (Nov 1917), believing it was composed 'especially for Korean youth' (actually a re-use of Fruit-Gathering no. 85)
travel_summary: Korea -> Japan (Tokyo/Yokohama 1916); never India
evidence_of_influence: kyosu.net (citing Cho Yong-man 1982); koreatimes 2019; dongne.donga.com D-story 32 (2009)
historical_significance: The first Korean to receive and publish a Tagore poem
notes: NULL

name_variants: Kim Uk; Kim Eok; pen name Anso (岸曙)
profession_role: Poet; translator (pioneer of Korean modern poetry translation); magazine editor
india_connection: Produced the first full Korean translation of Tagore's Gitanjali (『기탄자리』, Pyongyang: Imunkwan, March 1923), the landmark of Indian literature's arrival in Korea; his renderings later analysed for characteristic mistranslations (e.g., 'thou'->'king' devotional shift)
korea_connection: Founder-figure of Korean translation literature; introduced numerous world poets
travel_summary: No record of travel to India
evidence_of_influence: KCI scholarship: Jung Younghyo on Gitanjali/Kim Ŏk translation errors; Choi Dong-ho citing the March 1923 Pyongyang edition (National Assembly Library KINX2012046620; DBPia NODE01778075)
